newsitem.title: ITALY: Berlusconi hints at Italian no-confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: Berlusconi hints at Italian no-confidence vote.

text.p: Leader of the opposition Silvio Berlusconi on Monday raised the spectre of a possible no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Romano Prodi's government over the 1997 Italian budget.

Earlier on Monday, Berlusconi ally and leader of the hard-right National Alliance, Gianfranco Fini, suggested that the opposition should present a parliamentary motion of no-confidence against Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco.
Berlusconi, who served as prime minister for seven months in 1994, said he was personally opposed to motions of no-confidence against individual ministers.
"Our no-confidence, in reality, regards the entire government, which is bringing the country to ruin," he said in a statement. He did not say if he actually planned to present a no-confidence motion.

"This government is hard of hearing. It is not listening to the protests rising from nearly all sectors against a budget that is becoming always more oppressive, messy and unfair," the leader of the centre-right Freedom Alliance said.
Prime Minister Prodi last month unveiled an austerity budget designed to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($40 billion) off next year's deficit -- double the size of the originally planned package.
As part of the budget, Visco pledged to reform Italy's complex fiscal system and has already unveiled plans to introduce a new regional tax (Irep) aimed at corporates and self-employed workers.

He has drawn heavy flak from across the political spectrum for proposing to lift the minimum personal tax rate to 20 percent from the present 10 percent and reduce the top tax rate to 46 percent from 51 percent.

The government is also planning a once-off "Euro-Tax", which has yet to be outlined but is hoped to raise some 12.5 trillion lire next year, while efforts to hike property taxes have had to be scaled down in the face of widespread opposition.

"This government is targeting the middle classes, the productive sector, wage earners and professionals, merchants and artisans, those few who still have the will to be entrepreneurs and take risks in this dark and oppressive climate of recession," Berlusconi said in a statement.

Italy's centre-left government enjoys a full majority in the upper house of parliament (Senate) but has to rely upon the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation to control the Lower House of parliament.
Refoundation has called on Visco to scrap plans to increase the minimum personal tax rate.
